segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, so one of my co-workers, David Kestenbaum, started telling me about this thing. And really, I thought he was completely-- I just-- there was no way it could be true. It just seemed completely ridiculous. And then, I got to say, the more he explained, the more it slowly started to seem like, OK, maybe he's right.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Important fact to know about David before we go any further-- he has a PhD in physics, worked at Fermilab on subatomic particles, was on the team that discovered the top quark. And then this whole thing between him and me began when he told me to download an app onto my iPhone.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It's called Universe Splitter.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: [DING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, so now I've opened it up. And there's, like, a gray steel, fake steel background. And it says in white type on top of it, Universe Splitter, quantum-induced universe bifurcation. What do I do now?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: All right, so tell me something you are having trouble making up your mind about what to do.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You and I are recording this on December 31.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And I've had a week off. I grew a beard.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I noticed.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And I'm trying to decide if I should shave it off. And so that's something I'm trying to decide.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I have an opinion on that, but--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What's your opinion?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: [LAUGHS] Actually, I think it looks pretty good right now.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, so what does this Universe Splitter do?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It lets you do both. Like, it creates a duplicate of this universe so that in one you get to grow the beard, and in the other you shave it off.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wait, that's what we're going to do?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: For pretend or for real?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: No, no, for real, maybe. This is a thing. It's called the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics. And there are a lot of really smart physicists who think this is probably what's happening.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, so how does this work? Like, what do I do next?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: All right, so there are two boxes there?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah. In one box it says, In one universe, I will now.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: OK, so put, shave off beard tonight.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Hold on-- shave off beard tonight. OK, and then the other box is labeled, In the other universe. In the other one, I will now--

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Put keep beard.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Keep beard.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: OK. And then what's below it?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then below it there's like a button with like, an atom drawn on it.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: [LAUGHS] Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Like an atom like you would draw it in a 1950s cartoon.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Yeah, that's like the aesthetic of the whole thing. It's like an old piece of scientific equipment.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So what does it do when you push the button?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: So if you push the button, it sends a signal to a fancy piece of scientific equipment at the University of Geneva in Switzerland. And the equipment these days can be tiny, like a little box you can hold in your hand. And it does the following. It takes a single particle of light, a photon, it sends it at a kind of mirror that can make the photon either go left or right. You can think of it that way.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Like at random it'll go either left or right?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Well, according to the laws of quantum mechanics, which govern very small things, it actually goes both. It's not that we don't know. It actually goes left and right at the same time.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: So that's super weird, right? But that is actually true, and demonstrated, and like we've known that since the '20s.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK. So then what happens in this device in Geneva?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Yeah, so the device fires a photon which can go left or right. And then the device looks to see, well, where did it go? And we know the particle's in both places, right? But when the machine looks, it only finds it in one place. It shows it went either left or right, which doesn't make sense, right? Because we know from the math that the particle did go to both places. So why did we only see it in one of those places?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And what's the answer?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: All right, so one of the answers is that the photon is in both places, left and right, but just in different universes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wait. So you're saying that when you shoot the photon into the mirror, it actually creates an entire duplicate of our universe. And in one of those universes, the photon is on the left, and the other it is on the right?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Yes. It both went left and right. Those are just in different universes. The math of it makes a lot of-- the math of it is very, like, streamlined and simple. I remember the day I saw it in class, and I was like, oh, my god. Maybe it's true.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: So those boxes you filled out on the app--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You mean the box where I typed in "shave off beard tonight", and the box where I typed in, keep beard?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Right, right. So it'll basically choose one of those boxes if the photon goes left, and the other box if the photon goes right.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, got it.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: You have to do what it says.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You mean I have to keep the beard or shave off the beard like it tells me?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Yeah. Yeah, because when you press that button, you're going to get back one answer. But there's going to be a duplicate universe in which there is a duplicate you sitting in a duplicate studio and a duplicate me and you holding a duplicate phone in exactly the same way. The only difference is that that phone comes back with the other answer.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then that version of me will do whatever it says on the phone?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: We know that other guy. We trust him. He's going to go do the other.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, I think I understand all this. Let's go ahead.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Do you want to press the button?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah, go ahead. Push it.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: [LAUGHS] I do feel weird about it. I feel weird. I know it's crazy. I feel weird.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You literally just put your finger right up to the button and pulled it away in fear.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: All right, here it goes-- the split universe.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: [BEEP]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, it says, Input valid. Internet contacted. Geneva online. Device ready. Photon emitted. Quantum event.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [ROCKET BLASTING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Your universe has just split. You're in the universe in which you should keep beard. And right now in the other universe, the other you is being told to shave off beard tonight.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So after that, I kept the beard that night. And friends at New Year's parties asked me about it. And if the universe did in fact split, the other version of me in the other universe must have had different conversations. Maybe for instance somebody gave him a great idea for a show today that, in that universe, instead of airing this show, in that universe you're hearing a totally different theme.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And David, just to be sure I'm understanding this, you're saying this isn't a metaphor. You're saying there are scientists who really believe that a second universe gets created?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Yeah, for sure. I mean, I think it's not most physicists. And there are some who think it's ridiculous, for sure. But there are some would take it very seriously.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, where is this alternate universe that we're creating?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Yeah, I don't really even know how to think about this. But if this is true, the universe is duplicating itself all the time. It's like a fundamental thing about existence.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, today on our program, in a universe that may be duplicating itself all the time, we have people who have become entranced by the idea of a parallel universe out there where things are different. In one of those stories, things are better in the alternate world in one crucial way. In another story, two parallel worlds overlap. In another, a woman tries to visit-- she actually tries to go to the parallel universe. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act 1, Dreams From My Father. So I was e-mailing with a fiction writer that we have on our show sometimes, Etgar Keret, about today's theme. And he told me that his father used to spend a lot of time imagining worlds like we're talking about in today's program-- parallel worlds to ours that are almost the same as our world, but not quite. And he said his father did this starting during World War II. His father was 14, living in Poland-- he was Jewish-- when the Germans invaded and started sending Jews to the concentration camps.

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: During the Second World War, him and his parents, they hid in a hole in the ground that they dug for 620 days. So he had a lot of spare time.

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: And when he was there, he would imagine all kinds of things. He would imagine a world in which the Nazis didn't exist, or in which he wasn't a Jew, or in which people just in general didn't kill each other, you know? And this kind of thing was something that he associated with being a child. Then he kind of felt that it interested him as a child, then I will probably like it too.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Back during the war, his father couldn't leave that hole for almost two years. The Nazi headquarters was right there near the hole on the same property. A Christian farmer in his 80s would bring them food and haul out buckets of urine. They couldn't even talk a lot of the time. Etgar imagines it was like two years of meditation.

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: My father, the way that he would talk about his time in the hole, he would say that he would sleep, and then he would wake up, and then he would ask his father if the war was over. And his father would say no, so he would go and sleep some more. That's the way he would tell it to me. I think it's that kind of-- the softcore version.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And was it like, when you say a hole, could they even stand up?

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: No. They couldn't stand in it, and they couldn't even lie down in it. They had to sit in it. And when the Russians liberated the town and they were brought out, they had to be carried out because their muscles were so cramped that, by the time of the end of the war, they couldn't move them.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, my god. So basically they're in this hole, and they're sitting there?

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: Yes. And you know, it's like it's very, very cold, you know? It's way beyond freezing. And you don't have food. And you hear voices in German, and you know that you can easily be killed. And you close your eyes, and you think of another universe.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Etgar's written lots of fiction that imagines parallel worlds of various kinds. And when I asked him if he wanted to do something for today's show, he wrote this story-- a true story that starts when he was a kid.

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: When I was six years old, my dad worked at a pool snack bar not far from one of Tel Aviv's beaches. Every day at 5:30 in the morning he'd leave home for the pool, swim 2 kilometers, shower in the locker room, and get to work. He wouldn't get home till 9:00 at night. 14 hours a day, 7 days a week unloading boxes of soft drinks, dressing toasted sandwiches, brewing coffee in gleaming glasses at the pool snack bar up by the beach.

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: Years later, Dad always said those were the best days of his life, fondly remembering how the salty air blowing in from the sea would mix in his lungs with the smell of the coffee and the imported cigarettes he used to sell at the bar. Coffee, cigarettes, and the sea were always my father's three favorite things.

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: For me, those days were not quite as happy. When Dad came back from work, I was already in bed. And other than Saturdays when I'd go off to visit him at the pool with my mom, I never saw him at all. Not that I was bitter about this. Six-year-old children can't really imagine a different world for themselves, one where their father had more time for them. They accept reality as it is. And yet, I missed him dearly.

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: Seeing this, my mother suggested I go with him every morning to the pool, have a swim together, and take a cab to school from there. I don't remember anything of those morning swims, but the car rides with Dad are crystal clear.

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: It's still dark as we sit in our Silver Peugeot 504, the windows rolled down, Dad smoking Kent 100s and describing parallel universes that exist at this very moment in other dimensions-- universes where everything is precisely identical to ours-- same road, same traffic light, same cigarette in the corner of Dad's mouth-- all except for one tiny difference. And this difference Dad would change every morning, changing the one detail in the parallel universe that differed from ours.

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: Here we are in the parallel universe waiting at the exact same intersection for the light to change. Only in this universe, instead of a Silver Peugeot, we are riding a dragon. And here's another one where under my faded sweatpants hide gills which allow me to breathe under water like a fish.

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: When I was nine, my father got a new job. He no longer had to get up so early in the morning. And in the evenings, we'd all have dinner together and watch the nightly news. I was 22 by the time I moved out of my parents' house, but I still made sure to visit them at least twice a week. And on Saturdays, I'd swim with Dad at the pool where he once worked.

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: When I was 43, my father was diagnosed with cancer. It was tongue cancer, the result of 50 years of smoking. By the time the doctors caught on, it was at an advanced stage. And though we never spoke a word about it, it was obvious to us both that soon he was going to die.

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: On Mondays, I take him in for his physical therapy. And as we sat in the waiting room to see the physical therapist with the British accent, my father sometimes still talked about parallel universes where everything was exactly the same as ours, save for one difference-- say, that dogs could speak, or that people could read minds, or that the sky was purple. And when the milk white clouds floated across it, they looked tasty enough to eat.

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: At the end of every session, the physical therapist would show me how to hold my father's arm when we walked together and what I should do in case he lost his balance. On our way home as we approached the corner of King Solomon and Arlozorov, Dad would always stop. "Do you smell that?" he'd say, and point to the new cafe at the corner. "Just by the smell of it, I can tell you that's the best coffee in town."

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: At this stage of his illness, the tongue cancer was so advanced my father could no longer eat or drink. Instead, he got all his food and liquids through a clear plastic tube straight to his stomach. On one of these Mondays after physical therapy while walking by the corner cafe on King Solomon and Arlozorov, my father, instead of just posing to praise the place as usual, suggested we actually go in for a cup of coffee.

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: "Dad," I said after a moment's hesitation, "you can't drink anything. The tumor is blocking your esophagus." "I know," he said and patted me on the back, "but you can."

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: We sat at a corner table on the sidewalk. I ordered a latte and a glass of water from the pretty waitress. And when she asked my father what he'd like, he asked for a double espresso. I stared at him, confused, and he smiled and shrugged. The waitress noticed Dad's guilty smile and gave me a questioning look. Not knowing what to say, I ordered an oatmeal cookie.

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: Until the coffee arrived, we sat in silence. I wanted to ask my father why he'd ordered the coffee at all and if it had anything to do with the waitress being pretty, but I said nothing. Dad pulled a cigarette pack out of his shirt pocket and a lighter he had stored in his glasses case and set them both down on the table. We waited.

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: A few minutes later, the waitress returned with our order. She placed it on the table-- a latte, a glass of water, and a cookie in front of me, and a double espresso in front of Dad. Aromatic steam rose from my coffee. I wanted to drink it. But doing that in Dad's face seemed unfair, so I just kept staring at it.

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: When out of the corner of my eye, I saw my father quickly snatch the double espresso off the table and gulp it down in one sip. It was impossible. I knew it was impossible. After all, I was there in the room when the oncologists showed me and my mother the X-ray with the tumor resting above the blocked esophagus like a scoop of vanilla ice cream on a waffle cone.

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: My father, she said then, could never drink again. And here we were sitting together on a pleasant summer day at this hipster cafe, me still staring at my steaming cup of coffee, and him by my side, smiling after killing off his double espresso.

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: And for a moment there, I thought maybe we were in a parallel universe. Maybe he told me enough stories ever since I was a little boy to tear open a hole in the aching heart of our universe through which we were sucked into a parallel one, identical to our own in every way save for one exception. In this universe, my dad could drink and eat as much as he liked, and he was not about to die in just a few months.

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: The piping hot coffee slid down my father's windpipe and into his lungs. When it got there, Dad started to choke. He stood up and grabbed his throat with both hands. The wet wheezing noises he made were horrific-- the sound of a man whose lungs are flooded with hot coffee. A bespectacled man from the table next to us leaped up and asked my father if he needed any help.

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: I just sat there paralyzed. The parallel universe I had shared with my father moments ago had vanished, dropping me back into a far worse universe. A few more seconds of gargling followed, after which Dad leaned over and coughed up, evacuating all the fine Italian espresso that had filled his lungs.

segments.speaker: Etgar Keret
segments.text: When he was done, he sat up in his chair as if nothing had happened, inches away from the puddle of coffee and phlegm, and lit himself a cigarette. People at the tables around us kept staring at him. "What did I tell you?" He smiled at me and exhaled smoke from his nostrils. "The best coffee in town."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Etgar Keret. He's the author of many books. He writes about his dad and the rest of his family in stories a lot like this one-- emotional fables that happen to be true-- in his book, The Seven Good Years.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act 2, Sorry, Not Sorry. So it's kind of grim to say this, but the moon landing-- that story of American triumph-- it could've gone in another way. In some other storyline from the multiverse, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin, they land on the moon, they walk around, it's great. But then there's a problem, and they cannot take off to come home. NASA thought this was the most dangerous moment in the mission, the most likely spot it could fail.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: One of President Richard Nixon's speechwriters, William Safire, actually prepared a statement to be read in case that was the way the story went. At the top of the page in all caps it read, "In the event of moon disaster,"-- first line of the speech-- "fate has ordained that the men who went to the moon to explore it in peace will stay on the moon to rest in peace." Pretty good.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: David Kestenbaum has this next story about another presidential speech, never delivered, that also feels like it slipped into our world from a parallel universe. You can find this speech framed, hanging in the guest bathroom of a home in California. Here's David.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The speech was to be read on the night of August 17, 1998. It's in the house of Bob Shrum, because he wrote it. Shrum was a longtime Democratic political strategist, speechwriter, and getter-outer of tight spots.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Are you personally good at apologizing?

segments.speaker: Bob Shrum
segments.text: Oh, I've had to apologize so many times for so many things-- sure.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: What's the most recent thing you apologized for?

segments.speaker: Bob Shrum
segments.text: Having a fight with my wife about what we were giving various people as Christmas gifts.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: This story is about an apology he wrote for a much bigger audience. That August, 1998, Shrum was on vacation in Idaho staying with some friends, and the phone rang.

segments.speaker: Bob Shrum
segments.text: Well, I didn't have a cell phone then, so somehow or other-- oh, my office called me and said Mark was trying to reach me.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Mark is Mark Penn, who at the time was conducting polls and advising the President of the United States, who at the time was Bill Clinton, who at the time was in a lot of hot water.

segments.speaker: Mark Penn
segments.text: Impeachment might very well be an option-- tampering with witnesses, obstruction of justice are very, very serious charges.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: A moment when one political party said there were very valid high crimes and misdemeanors, and the other party said that's ridiculous political posturing. Anyway, there had been stories in the press for months at this point that Clinton might have had an affair with an intern, Monica Lewinsky. Clinton denied it, though, under oath in a civil case, and famously on television.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: [CAMERAS CLICKING]

segments.speaker: Bill Clinton
segments.text: But I want to say one thing to the American people. I want you to listen to me. I'm going to say this again. I did not have sexual relations with that woman, Miss Lewinsky.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: But there was the dress with Clinton's DNA on it and recorded phone calls between Monica Lewinsky and a co-worker talking about the affair. At the time Bob Shrum got the call, President Clinton was finally going to have to testify before independent counsel Ken Starr's grand jury. He would have to own up to the affair, and then afterwards say something to the nation. But what?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: That was what the phone call was about. Shrum called Mark Penn back, who asked if he would take a shot at writing a speech for the president to be delivered on TV just after he gave his grand jury testimony. It would be the president's chance to frame the whole thing, maybe finally put it away and prevent the Republicans from starting impeachment proceedings. The country would be watching. Bob Shrum said OK. He hung up the phone and told his wife and the couple they were staying with on vacation what the assignment was.

segments.speaker: Bob Shrum
segments.text: One of the people there said, this better be good.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Meaning you better do a good job?

segments.speaker: Bob Shrum
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Bob Shrum
segments.text: So I sat at the dining room table and I wrote in longhand on a yellow pad, which is how I've always written. I drafted it.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: What he wrote was a straight up, direct apology.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Do you have it there with you?

segments.speaker: Bob Shrum
segments.text: It's on the-- well, actually, I can go get it. You want to hold on for a second?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Shrum went to go get it from where it was hanging in what he calls the guest powder room. And to be clear, there's other political memorabilia in there. It's a speech he's proud of.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Can you read the speech for me?

segments.speaker: Bob Shrum
segments.text: Yeah. It's not very long, so I will.

segments.speaker: Bob Shrum
segments.text: "My fellow Americans, no one who is not in my position can understand fully the remorse I feel today. Since I was very young, I have had a profound reverence for this office I hold. I've been honored that you, the people, have entrusted it to me. I am proud of what we have accomplished together.

segments.speaker: Bob Shrum
segments.text: But in this case, I have fallen short of what you should expect from a president. I have failed my own religious faith and values. I have let too many people down. I take full responsibility for my actions-- for hurting my wife and daughter, for hurting Monica Lewinsky and her family, for hurting friends and staff, and for hurting the country I love. None of this ever should have happened."

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Then he has Clinton apologizing for misleading people about the affair. And this is how it ends.

segments.speaker: Bob Shrum
segments.text: "Finally, I also want to apologize to all of you, my fellow citizens. I hope that you can find it in your heart to accept my apology. I pledge to you that I will make every effort of mind and spirit to earn your confidence again, to be worthy of this office, and to finish the work on which we have made such remarkable progress in the past six years. God bless you, and good night."

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: How does it feel reading that?

segments.speaker: Bob Shrum
segments.text: I mean, I remember writing it. I thought it was the right thing for him to say. And when I hear it now, I still think it's the right thing for him to say.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It's notable that Shrum had the president apologizing to Monica Lewinsky and her family. At the time, Charles Rangel, the Democratic congressman from New York, called her, quote, "a young tramp."

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: She was the subject of jokes on late night television. Bill Maher said, "I think Monica Lewinsky is the one who should apologize to America." No one seemed to be thinking about her as a person whose life was now a wreck. Shrum was.

segments.speaker: Bob Shrum
segments.text: Well, I mean, she was an intern, a kid in the White House. And I thought that that made every bit of sense in the world.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Shrum sent the speech into the White House. And then the day arrived. Clinton gave his grand jury testimony, which was not broadcast. And that evening, the president went on TV to give his speech. Shrum sat down with the rest of the country to watch it.

segments.speaker: Bob Shrum
segments.text: We were just sitting around in the living room, watching it on television.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: And at that point are you thinking, maybe he's going to read my speech?

segments.speaker: Bob Shrum
segments.text: Sure. I thought he might very well-- Bill Clinton, who I worked with on State of the Union messages, never exactly reads what you send him. So I didn't anticipate that it would be necessarily word for word what I had sent, but I thought it might be pretty close to it. It was almost diametrically the opposite.

segments.speaker: Bill Clinton
segments.text: Good evening. This afternoon in this room, from this chair, I testified before the office of independent counsel and the grand jury. I answered their questions truthfully, including questions about my private life, questions no American citizen would ever want to answer.

segments.speaker: Bob Shrum
segments.text: I not only remember hearing the first words, but I remember the look on his face. He was really, really angry. It's the private Bill Clinton who could get angry. And I have seen him angry, but I don't think the country had seen him angry very often.

segments.speaker: Bill Clinton
segments.text: As you know, in a deposition in January, I was asked questions about my relationship with Monica Lewinsky. While my answers were legally accurate, I did not volunteer information. Indeed, I did have a relationship with Miss Lewinsky that was not appropriate. In fact, it was wrong. It constituted a critical lapse in judgment and a personal failure on my part for which I am solely and completely responsible.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: There are moments of apology in there and what feel like honest reflection, like when he straight up admits the reasons he had been so evasive until then.

segments.speaker: Bill Clinton
segments.text: I can only tell you I was motivated by many factors-- first, by a desire to protect myself from the embarrassment of my own conduct.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: But the overall message is not I'm sorry. I screwed up, he seems to be saying, but the real problem is the fact that I'm having to talk about this at all. It's a private family matter.

segments.speaker: Bill Clinton
segments.text: It's nobody's business but ours. Even presidents have private lives.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: He closes not by asking for forgiveness, as Shrum had advised, but by asking people to stop gawking.

segments.speaker: Bill Clinton
segments.text: And so tonight, I ask you to turn away from the spectacle of the past seven months, to repair the fabric of our national discourse, and to return our attention to all the challenges and all the promise of the next American century. Thank you for watching, and good night.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: What do you think would have happened if instead that night he'd taken out your speech and read it?

segments.speaker: Bob Shrum
segments.text: I think it would have lessened the chances that he would've been impeached.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Bob Shrum
segments.text: I don't know that it would have prevented the impeachment, but I think it would have lessened the chances.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It's possible his speech gets you to the same ending, just with a slightly different plot. And after all, there was a lot of momentum in Congress toward impeachment. But it's nice to contemplate a world where the leader of your country can stand up and acknowledge having made a mistake, can acknowledge reality.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: An apology really is about the truth-- laying it out so we can all live in the same world together. It's impossible to imagine that happening now. Clinton seemed closer to it at that moment, but he still couldn't do it.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I wonder, of all the possible universes, in how many of them does Clinton say I'm sorry, you know? Not I'm sorry for what happened, or I'm sorry if people feel-- but really like I'm sorry.

segments.speaker: Bob Shrum
segments.text: There may be a universe in which he did that. I'm just not aware of it, because I don't live in it.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: [LAUGHS] Yeah, that's not the one we live in.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You want to know what I think? I think it's possible there is no universe in which President Clinton reads Bob Shrum's speech. Listening to the speech Clinton did give, I kind of think he gives it in every possible universe. It was exactly how he felt.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: And the speech that you wrote, while great, was not at all how he was feeling at that moment.

segments.speaker: Bob Shrum
segments.text: Obviously, the speech that I drafted did not reflect how he felt coming out of the grand jury.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: In that sense, can you fault him?

segments.speaker: Bob Shrum
segments.text: I just think you want to do what fits the moment, and you want to be true to yourself. The problem was that, I think, he was true to the angry guy who had just come out of the room, you know? He was maybe not true to the person he was the next day.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: There are the yous in all the parallel worlds, but also the you on Thursday and the one on Friday, the one who's had some time to think, and some sleep, and a sandwich. For sure, those are different people.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: David Kestenbaum. In some other universe, he stayed a physicist for all of his life. In this one, he is the executive editor of our program.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Bill Clinton, by the way, later wrote about this address to the nation that night in his biography. He does not mention Shrum's draft of the speech, but he does say that most of his advisors had counseled him to simply admit that he had made an awful mistake-- not to go out swinging. He did anyway, of course.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Weeks after that speech, he backtracked in front of a smaller audience at a prayer breakfast with religious leaders. He took a different tone there. He said, "I agree with those who have said that in my first statement after I testified I was not contrite enough." It was much closer to what Shrum had written. He included an apology to Monica Lewinsky and her family.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Coming up, worried that you're living in a parallel universe where some very basic facts about your own life have been altered? That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We've arrived at Act 3 of our show, Act 3-- Sklar-Crossed Brothers.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So if you think about it, being an identical twin is kind of a parallel world situation. You know, you have this other version of yourself stuck in the same world as you, stuck in the same house as you. You see somebody who's just like you running around, doing things that you might not do.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Dana Chivvis has this next story about a mother, her twins, and a 48-year-old mystery.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Annette Sklar had a lot going on in the winter of '72. In January, she delivered twin boys-- Jason first, followed by Randy 5 minutes later. Weighing 5 pounds, 2 ounces, Randy had to spend the first days of life in an incubator.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: They lived in suburban St. Louis. Annette's husband Dick had a job at a paper company, called Tension Envelope. He worked long hours and traveled a lot. Annette was often at home alone caring for two infants-- feeding them, changing diapers, and making sure she didn't lose track of which one was which, because they looked exactly alike.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Were you always scared that you might mix them up? Like from the day they were born, was that a real fear?

segments.speaker: Annette Sklar
segments.text: I tried to be really careful about knowing who either had-- what outfit they were on. I knew-- I was really careful about it. So usually, we had outfits in different colors-- blue, blue Jay, and red, Randy red. And then I didn't think about it too much, once I knew it was.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Annette Sklar
segments.text: [LAUGHS] That's how we did it.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: That's a good system.

segments.speaker: Annette Sklar
segments.text: I mean, I think I did feed them twice, one of them, and didn't feed the other one. That happens, sometimes. You did that. You did that. One of them was eating, the other one was crying a lot. And I go, why is he crying so much?

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: She even had a back-up-- a creative redundancy she built into the safety plan for their identities. And that was diaper pins. She used blue diaper pins for Jason, and yellow ones for Randy.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Everything went smoothly for a while. And then at six weeks, they had their first check-up. Annette dressed them in the same outfit-- a fancy number their aunt in Los Angeles had sent them. But underneath the clothes, the diaper pin system was up and running.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: At the doctor's office, a nurse took the babies out of the room. Annette can't really remember why. Maybe she needed to weigh them. And a few minutes later, the nurse came back in with the boys.

segments.speaker: Annette Sklar
segments.text: And she goes, oh, we have such a great surprise for you. Now we have Pampers. We're just using them for the first time. So instead of using your diapers, we used your Pampers.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Oh, no.

segments.speaker: Annette Sklar
segments.text: And then they gave me all four of their tins.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: The nurse had changed the babies out of their cloth diapers and put them into disposable ones, foiling the system entirely. She handed Annette a little bag with the diaper pins in it. The boys were completely indistinguishable.

segments.speaker: Annette Sklar
segments.text: I was very upset. So they go, oh, you're going to be fine. You're fine. Of course, they go, you're fine. And we got in the car, and I was so upset the whole way home.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: When she got home, Annette put the babies on the couch and stared at them. At six weeks old, they didn't have distinct personalities yet. They weighed the same amount. They had the same bald heads. No birthmarks.

segments.speaker: Annette Sklar
segments.text: And I'm not kidding you, they looked exactly alike. And so I was thinking I was a really terrible mother.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Oh, no.

segments.speaker: Annette Sklar
segments.text: Then how can I really look at this and not see my own children and not know which ones they are?

segments.speaker: Linda Wallace
segments.text: You know, she called me in a panic. And she just said, I don't know what I'm going to do. I don't know which one's which. I don't know what to do.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: This is Annette's best friend Linda Wallace-- Aunt Linda, as Jason and Randy know her. She lived in the same subdivision.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Did you go over there to try to help her?

segments.speaker: Linda Wallace
segments.text: No, I didn't.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Linda Wallace
segments.text: Because if she couldn't tell them apart, how would I be able to tell them apart?

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Linda Wallace
segments.text: I mean, I couldn't tell them apart, you know? She had the pins.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Yeah. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Were you nervous to tell Dick? Were you nervous to tell your husband?

segments.speaker: Annette Sklar
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: You were?

segments.speaker: Annette Sklar
segments.text: Yes. I was really nervous. So when he came home, and he saw them, and they were in their crib-- and so finally, I had to tell him. I go, I have to tell you what happened. And I told him. And he goes, really? He goes, oh, we'll figure it out. Let's see.

segments.speaker: Annette Sklar
segments.text: And then we were both looking at both of them right next to each other. And then of course, they had the Pampers on, and nothing. And he's going, I don't know. What do you think it is? (LAUGHING) I go, I don't know.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Annette was faced with a decision. She had to choose which baby was Jason and which one was Randy. She had nothing to go on but a maternal feeling, so she chose. Dick agreed with her.

segments.speaker: Annette Sklar
segments.text: I really, always felt like I had the right person in my heart. I just said it is, and I'm not going to think about it anymore. This is my life. We know who they are, and it is who they are. And we're not going to talk about it anymore.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Aunt Linda? Not so convinced.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Do you think she got it right? Do you think Annette got it right?

segments.speaker: Linda Wallace
segments.text: I don't know.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: You don't know?

segments.speaker: Linda Wallace
segments.text: I mean, I don't think she knows. She says she did, but how does she know? I mean, there's no way. They were so-- they looked so much alike, and so I'm not sure.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Jason and Randy are 48 years old now. They're comedians. They work together. They've done cameos on different TV shows, like Curb Your Enthusiasm and Better Call Saul. And they still look exactly the same.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Randy, can you describe what Jason looks like?

segments.speaker: Randy Sklar
segments.text: He's very good looking. Jason, he is very Semitic looking. He's got glasses. He's about 5 foot, 8 and 1/2.

segments.speaker: Jason Sklar
segments.text: That's generous.

segments.speaker: Randy Sklar
segments.text: Somewhat athletic looking.

segments.speaker: Jason Sklar
segments.text: Less generous.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: They found out about their potentially swapped identities when they were about 12 years old, by accident. They were spending a summer weekend at the world famous Lake of the Ozarks in central Missouri with their mom and Aunt Linda and her two sons. The boys were playing while Annette and Aunt Linda talked amongst themselves. The story of the calamitous doctor's visit came up. And unbeknownst to them, Jason and Randy were in earshot, and they overheard the whole thing.

segments.speaker: Jason Sklar
segments.text: And we were just-- we hated the story.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: This is Jason. He sounds remarkably like Randy.

segments.speaker: Jason Sklar
segments.text: We were livid that this could have happened, and also that she was sharing it in sort of an offhand kind of joking way. And Linda Wallace, who is a funny woman, was making it funnier. And they were laughing about it. And we were like-- we were just very embarrassed by it and upset by it. Like, oh my god, this is an insane thing to hear, because we may not be who we are.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: What pissed you off about it? What was so upsetting about it?

segments.speaker: Jason Sklar
segments.text: I think that it just was we were just sensitive, I think, to being confused. And again, it was this narrative that kind of went through our lives, as we wanted to be individuals and we wanted to be seen as individuals. And then here's this thing that happened where we could be so easily confused.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: For identical twins-- two people who are constantly being mistaken for one another, who try really hard to make it clear that they're unique individuals-- this was a big deal. Randy was the most upset.

segments.speaker: Annette Sklar
segments.text: He goes, why can't you go to the policemen? I think Randy really wanted me to go there. We were talking all the way to the car.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Not that an actual crime had been committed, just a crime against their dignity. But for some reason, Randy figured the police were the ones who could sort it out. But Annette did not go to the police. And the name confusion did not get sorted out, it remained a mystery in Jason and Randy's lives.

segments.speaker: Linda Wallace
segments.text: The couple times that it was brought up throughout their years, if somebody said something about it, they would go, I don't want to hear about it. Don't bring it up again.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Wow. I had no idea it was that painful for them.

segments.speaker: Linda Wallace
segments.text: I mean, it was a joke between Annette and I that I'm not sure was a joke between all of us, because they were very sensitive about it.

segments.speaker: Randy Sklar
segments.text: Just the simple fact of the matter that for countless times in our lives, someone has said to me, Jason? And I'm like, nope, I'm Randy.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Randy Sklar
segments.text: You know? Like, that that's happened so many times in my life. If that's not true, there is--

segments.speaker: Jason Sklar
segments.text: You have to go back to every single one of those people and apologize.

segments.speaker: Randy Sklar
segments.text: --and apologize. No, but there's a notion that you've been living a little bit of a lie. It's a tiny lie, but it's not your lie.

segments.speaker: Jason Sklar
segments.text: Not your lie.

segments.speaker: Randy Sklar
segments.text: It's not your lie, and it's not your fault. But still, that's unsettling in a weird way, to me. That's just weird that for all this time I had it wrong.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: If they were switched, then they have to re-imagine something that's so foundational nobody ever thinks about it-- their birth. Who's older? Who was in the incubator? Like Randy says, it's weird. It doesn't really make a difference, but also somehow it does. And not knowing what the truth is, that's even more unnerving.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: It turns out there was one way to figure it out. Sometime around the age of 40-- Randy can't remember exactly when-- the topic of their potentially swapped identities came up. And they were like, why haven't we figured this out yet? They were grown ass adults. They should know who they actually were. And also, they were working as comedians at that point, and they thought it might be good material, which-- we'll see.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Randy thought maybe the hospital where they were born would have a copy of their baby fingerprints. They could get those and compare them to their adult fingerprints. He wasn't wrong about the science part of that. Identical twins have nearly the same DNA, so their fingerprint patterns are very similar-- closer than anyone else's.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: As you probably know, fingerprints are made up of lines. And some of those lines have tiny variations in them, like forks or loops. And those markings are different between identical twins. For those of you still listening, the reason for that is that the markings develop based on the conditions in the womb, like pressure, which is different depending on where the baby is in the womb.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: So Randy called the hospital where they were born to see if they still had a copy of their fingerprints. The hospital told them that they throw birth records out after 30 years. They were old and out of luck.

segments.speaker: Randy Sklar
segments.text: Until I was back home last summer with my family--

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: This is Randy.

segments.speaker: Randy Sklar
segments.text: --and I was digging through, just looking at stuff--

segments.speaker: Jason Sklar
segments.text: In St. Louis.

segments.speaker: Randy Sklar
segments.text: --in St. Louis. I was back in our childhood home that we had lived in since we were four years old. And I found from the hospital our footprints. I couldn't believe it.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Where were they?

segments.speaker: Randy Sklar
segments.text: They were in a book--

segments.speaker: Jason Sklar
segments.text: A chest--

segments.speaker: Randy Sklar
segments.text: --inside of the--

segments.speaker: Jason Sklar
segments.text: --next to your bed, right?

segments.speaker: Randy Sklar
segments.text: Next to my bed, there was like a nightstand thing that was like a chest that you could open up. And it was just in the bottom of that. I couldn't believe it. And I'd never seen it there before. And I thought, OK, we could find out. It became more real.

segments.speaker: Jason Sklar
segments.text: Real, and the possibility was rekindled.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: If they could find someone to compare their adult footprints to their baby footprints, maybe they could put this mystery to bed once and for all. As luck would have it, there was just such a person in Buena Park, California, about 25 miles from Los Angeles where Jason and Randy now live-- a forensic identification specialist by the name of Kurt Kuhn.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: But Kurt said there was no way he could use a baby footprint from a hospital. Those aren't made for identification purposes, they're made because baby feet are freaking cute. They're mementos, and they usually don't have much detail.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: In June, Jason sent Kurt the footprints anyway, just to check. And when Kurt saw them, he confirmed that they were mostly just unusable smudges of ink. But miraculously, there was a half-inch spot on the ball of the left Jason foot that had nice, clear lines. He shouldn't have any problem making the identification. He just needed Jason and Randy's adult feet.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Faced with the imminent revelation of their true identities, Jason and Randy were forced to think through what they would actually do if they'd been switched as babies, which, let's be honest, is not a long list of considerations.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Do you think you'd swap names?

segments.speaker: Randy Sklar
segments.text: Or would we legally change our names to each other's names?

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Right. If you are swapped, then you're kind of like committing fraud all the time right now.

segments.speaker: Randy Sklar
segments.text: I guess, yeah.

segments.speaker: Jason Sklar
segments.text: Unintentionally.

segments.speaker: Randy Sklar
segments.text: Unintentional fraud, yeah. Well, I would be using his social security number.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Randy Sklar
segments.text: You know, how does that affect everything we do?

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: I wonder if it does. I mean, maybe it only matters if one of you commits murder barefoot, and then runs through wet cement or something.

segments.speaker: Randy Sklar
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Maybe practically, it doesn't actually matter.

segments.speaker: Jason Sklar
segments.text: That one's out. We can't do that.

segments.speaker: Randy Sklar
segments.text: We can't do that now. Thanks a lot.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Maybe it doesn't matter. I'm probably right about that. Except there's one person who Jason was legitimately worried about-- their mom, Annette, who they're very close with. Their father died in 2009. Annette's had two strokes in recent years. They're protective of her. What if she got it wrong all those years ago?

segments.speaker: Jason Sklar
segments.text: I would feel bad for our mom.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Yeah, say more about that.

segments.speaker: Jason Sklar
segments.text: I would feel like maybe she would be embarrassed, or maybe she would feel like she should have spoken up and maybe found out a way in that moment to get our footprints and just dispel it and figure it out.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Annette, however, was not concerned.

segments.speaker: Annette Sklar
segments.text: I just have a feeling, that's all-- my feeling, my definite feeling that I know who's who. I know who you are. I'm the mother. I know.

segments.speaker: Randy Sklar
segments.text: What if it's different? You want me to change my name? What if I became Jason and Jason became me?

segments.speaker: Annette Sklar
segments.text: Then you have to have different girlfriends.

segments.speaker: Annette Sklar
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Randy Sklar
segments.text: You mean wives? Mom.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: A few days before Thanksgiving, I flew to LA and met Randy, Jason, and Annette at Randy's house where Annette was spending the holiday. We left her at home with her grandchildren and headed down the 5 towards Buena Park, and hopefully resolution. Randy said he was feeling remarkably zen. But Jason?

segments.speaker: Jason Sklar
segments.text: I feel more nervous today than ever before about this. Like, I think when we got into this, I was like, oh, this is going to be so interesting and fascinating. But I really want my mom to be right. Like, I want to be me. I don't know. I just woke up this morning saying, god, I hope my mom was right.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: We turned off the highway, drove through the gates of Kurt's subdivision, and pulled up to a house with a Winnebago out front.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Oh, it's a Winnebago.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The garage door was halfway down, and behind it we could see a pair of white legs that ended in a sock tan and flip-flops.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Kurt?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The garage door lifted to reveal Kurt--

segments.speaker: Jason Sklar
segments.text: What's up?

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: --a tall man with a full mustache and a voice like a cartoon bear.

segments.speaker: Kurt Kuhn
segments.text: And you're not coming in through the garage. Get on the front porch. Let me get rid of the trash and take them--

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: All right.

segments.speaker: Randy Sklar
segments.text: Done. Done and doner.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: We stepped into Kurt's living room, met his wife and granddaughter.

segments.speaker: Jason Sklar
segments.text: Hey, I'm Jason. Nice to meet you.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: We made an impressive amount of small talk about Thanksgiving, Winnebagos, hunting.

segments.speaker: Kurt Kuhn
segments.text: Well, have you ever bitten into birdshot while eating?

segments.speaker: Jason Sklar
segments.text: I have not, no.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: I have, actually.

segments.speaker: Kurt Kuhn
segments.text: So-- [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Kurt spent 25 and a half years working as a forensic identification specialist for the Beverly Hills and Los Angeles Police Departments.

segments.speaker: Jason Sklar
segments.text: There it is right there, yep.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: He shows us Jason and Randy's baby footprints. He'd had them locked in his safe for five months.

segments.speaker: Kurt Kuhn
segments.text: Take those.

segments.text: Act 4, If I Lived Here, I'd Be Home Now. So our last story today is about somebody who tries to visit a parallel world, one that she almost lived in herself. Diane Wu explains.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: The universe Emily ended up in was like a postcard for old-timey America-- 10 acres in Vermont with five big brothers and sisters eating candy out of glass jars at the family general store.

segments.speaker: Emily
segments.text: Yeah, we just lived in this big house. And my parents were really strict. [LAUGHS] My parents were so strict. They always reminded me of the Von Trapp family, even though that's really extreme.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: She almost lived a totally different life. Emily was adopted from South Korea when she was a baby. She's 40 now. And as a kid, she rarely thought about the world she came from, what her life would have been like there. It was the '80s. That kind of thing wasn't especially encouraged. Her family raised her not to ask many questions about her past, but there was one thing she really wanted to know about it.

segments.speaker: Emily
segments.text: I mean, mostly growing up I just really wondered what my birth mother looked like.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.text: That was usually the question that always came to my mind.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Her adoptive parents didn't look like her. They were white, as was most everybody else in town, so it was hard for her to picture her birth mother's face. But there was no one to ask.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: A couple of decades later, Emily became a mother herself and suddenly, felt connected to and curious about her birth mother again. She started researching how to contact her and, two long years later, finally got in touch.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Then she decided to go on a trip to South Korea to meet her birth mother-- a trip that would allow her to tunnel between the universe that was into the universe that might have been. She recorded parts of it for a podcast called, Motherhood Sessions. All of Emily's emotions about the trip hit her on the way to the airport in New York when suddenly she found herself sobbing while talking to the cab driver.

segments.text: She called the adoption agency several times over the years to check in on her daughter. Learned she'd been adopted by an American family. I talked with her on the phone. segments.text: Seeing her birth mother's face, meeting her whole extended family later on that trip, it had a profound impact on Emily. I heard her talk about it on that podcast, Motherhood Sessions. And I was surprised and moved to hear her say that being in the same room with her birth family--

segments.speaker: Emily
segments.text: For the first time, I felt pretty, you know? Because growing up, your parents always tell you that you're pretty, or whatever. But I never really believed it. segments.text: Because after growing up, living a lifetime of feeling like you don't fit in and wondering why maybe certain guys don't like you, or why maybe you're not the most popular person in school. segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Emily stayed with her birth family for three days in a town called Dongducheon in a little house by the railroad tracks. There were ceramic pots of kimchi in the yard, a flat screen TV in the living room that was always playing Korean variety shows and soap operas. Lots of visitors came by to welcome Emily. It felt warm, familiar.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: On the first night, Emily was getting ready for bed, and her birth mother came in and presented her with four boxes containing gold jewelry for Emily, her kids, and her husband. Emily accepted them, hesitantly. Then using a translation app, her birth mother told her--

segments.speaker: Emily
segments.text: She said Korean mothers sleep with their children. And I'm like, oh, god, here we go.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Emily had heard about this-- that it's not unusual for Korean parents to sleep in the same room as their kids, even when they're adults. In this room, there was only one bed. She tried to explain to her birth mother, sorry, but I prefer to sleep alone. It wasn't clicking. Emily ended up calling an interpreter she'd hired who had already gone home for the day.

segments.speaker: Emily
segments.text: And so I called her and asked her to explain that I couldn't do it. And she did, but you could see that my birth mother was pissed and not really happy about it. She had missed years and years of my life. I can understand why she'd want to sleep in the same room with me, but I just couldn't do it.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: A lot of the time with her birth mother was like this. As a visitor, it was impossible to fit in completely. She was a stranger and family all at the same time, dropping into a place that really felt like it could be home-- but it wasn't.
